ProbabilityTheory.independent_copies3_no.statement: Let $X_1:\Omega_1\to G_1$, $X_2:\Omega_2\to G_2$, $X_3:\Omega_3\to G_3$ be measurable (with finite range) on spaces with measures $\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3$. Then there exist a measurable space $A$, a probability measure $\mu_A$ on $A$ and measurable maps $X_1',X_2',X_3'$ on $A$ that are jointly independent under $\mu_A$, such that $X_i'$ under $\mu_A$ has the same distribution as $X_i$ under $\mu_i$ for $i=1,2,3$, and each $X_i'$ has finite range.
ProbabilityTheory.independent_copies3_no.sketch: Take the independent copies given by independent_copies3_nondep; each copy agrees in law with a finite-range variable, so it takes values in the finite range of the original almost surely, and one modifies it on a null set (preserving independence and identical distribution) to obtain a variable with finite range.

ProbabilityTheory.independent_copies_fin.statement:
Let $X:\Omega	o G$ and $Y:\Omega'	o G'$ be measurable (with finite range), and $\mu,\mu'$ measures on $\Omega,\Omega'$. Then there exist a probability measure $
u$ on some space and measurable maps $X',Y'$ on it such that $X'$ and $Y'$ are independent under $
u$, $X'$ under $
u$ has the same distribution as $X$ under $\mu$, $Y'$ under $
u$ has the same distribution as $Y$ under $\mu'$, and both $X'$ and $Y'$ have finite range.
ProbabilityTheory.independent_copies_fin.sketch: Take the independent copies from independent_copies; since they are identically distributed with finite-range variables they almost surely take values in the finite ranges of the originals, and are modified on a null set to have finite range while keeping independence and distributions.
